title: Japan Waives $21B for Two New York Fabs and Keeps None of the Equity, While Washington Takes 7%
subhead: Japan's money is building two GlobalFoundries plants in Malta, New York — but the US government owns 7% of the operator, Japan owns nothing, and Abu Dhabi's Mubadala still controls the company. A chip alliance where money, equity and authority sit in three different countries.

sections.heading: Japan funds, Washington owns, Abu Dhabi controls
sections.body:
GlobalFoundries confirmed on October 14 that Japan will invest up to $21 billion in two chip factories at its Malta, New York site, jointly owned by the US government and Japanese interests and operated by GlobalFoundries, per Reuters. The deal sits inside the 2025 Trump administration agreement under which Japan pledged $550 billion in US investment in exchange for tariffs on Japanese cars and other imports dropping from at least 25% to 15%.

The structure is unusual by design. GlobalFoundries CEO Tim Breen told Reuters the US government's stake will rise from 3% to 7%, valued by President Trump at more than $2 billion on the back of $1.63 billion in prior CHIPS grants. Japan provides all of the capital. GlobalFoundries pays no construction bill; it collects fees for at least 20 years — roughly $50 million next year alone for managing phase one — plus licensing income. 247WallSt notes the fee structure and the precise size of the government stake have not been disclosed.

About $10 billion is tied to the first fab, expected to produce chips in 2029 with site work beginning later in 2026; the second carries roughly $10 billion more and a decision by end-2028. At full operation each would add about 900,000 300mm wafers a year, putting the first among the larger US fabs, and create more than 1,000 factory jobs. First customers named by the company: Renesas, Apple, Cirrus Logic and General Motors — power, analog, radio and sensor chips on mature nodes, not AI accelerators.

One more layer of ownership: Abu Dhabi's Mubadala remains GlobalFoundries' majority shareholder. Japanese Trade Minister Ryosei Akazawa rejected criticism that the arrangement makes Japan subservient to Washington, saying projects undergo bilateral review for financial viability and benefit to Japanese firms. Breen added that at least some Japanese capital will flow back to Japanese toolmakers such as Tokyo Electron.
sections.whyItMatters: Japan is buying supply-chain security with no equity and no operational role, while the US converts old grants into an ownership stake and Abu Dhabi keeps control of the operator. Each government is getting a different thing from the same factory: Tokyo gets capacity and access, Washington gets a claim on upside, Mubadala gets fees and no depreciation. That is a durable arrangement only as long as all three want the same output.

sections.heading: GMO asks Japan to fire the first shot under its new cyber defense law — Tokyo hesitates
sections.body:
GMO Internet Group asked the Japanese government on October 24 to invoke the Active Cyber Defense Law on its behalf after an intrusion that spread far beyond one company. GMO first disclosed the breach on October 21: attackers planted malware in its Onamae.com Desktop Cloud Windows VPS service and the company said roughly 26,739 servers were potentially affected, per its CEO's account.

According to CEO Masatoshi Kumagai's October 25 blog post, the attackers did not stop at data theft — they placed unauthorized trades on customer accounts at more than 70 brokerage and securities firms in Japan and abroad, and threatened to leak personal data, deploy ransomware and publish internal GMO system information. GMO pledged a flat ¥5,000 payment per affected customer, full compensation for trading losses even where brokers refuse, six months of free replacement hosting, and an outside-led rearchitecture.

The government's answer was no automatic trigger. Per BigGo's reporting on the decision, a senior official said 'we do not trigger measures simply because a request is made,' and the National Cyber Security Office said there is no mechanism for accepting company requests — Tokyo will weigh severity and urgency itself. The law, in force since October 1, lets police and the Self-Defense Forces access attacker servers to remove malware or disable command functions, with prior approval from a third-party oversight committee, and the government will not disclose whether it acted. Keio University's Taiyo Tsuchiya said GMO's request 'differs from the neutralizing measures envisioned,' while the Sasakawa Peace Foundation's Jun Osawa warned that from the other state's perspective the measure 'could look like an act of war.'

The context Kumagai cited is a change in attack economics. He said open-weight AI models are being assembled into attack tooling, and that GMO's own defensive pentesting tool ARTEX was abused against roughly 20 Japanese companies. He described an 'AI cyber-saturation attack' in which volume, not skill, overwhelms defenders. Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 separately reported AI-agent-style post-exploitation against a European government entity that reached password hashes and MFA secrets within two hours of initial exploitation (see below).
sections.whyItMatters: Japan's first test of offensive cyber defense is a case the law was not written for: a private company asking the state to counterattack on its behalf, with no public record either way. If Tokyo declines, the deterrent value of a law it spent years building is weakened. If it acts and stays silent, it takes a step other states can call an armed attack with no accountability at home.

sections.heading: AI-made attacks are now an infrastructure problem, not a corporate one
sections.body:
Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 reported that after exploiting the critical PHP2Shell flaws (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619), attackers used agentic AI platforms for post-exploitation — and against a European government entity reached password hashes and multi-factor authentication secrets within two hours, established an NTLM-relay tunnel into Active Directory and attempted Domain Admin escalation. The tell, per Unit 42: command batches wrapped in delimiters like ==SHELLUSER== and ==PASSWD==, machine-parseable output built for a model to read.

CYFIRMA said it uncovered a suspected North Korea-linked campaign using PHP2Shell to probe global PHP infrastructure from 21 compromised nodes, with scanning 'deliberately low-volume and paced,' rotating nodes at the first sign of rate-limiting. The target list: 216 unpatched or partly mitigated hosts across the US, Japan, South Korea, Thailand, Indonesia, Australia, Taiwan, India, Singapore, the UAE, Saudi Arabia and the EU — spanning government, banks, logistics, airports and aviation, manufacturing and online transaction platforms. Attribution is at moderate confidence to a Korean-speaking operator in the Lazarus Group ecosystem; CYFIRMA cites Munhwaŏ orthography in the captured traffic.

The exposure is broad. Bitsight counts nearly 37 million internet-facing systems running PHP or PHP-related software, concentrated in the US, Germany, France, the Netherlands and Japan. Cloudflare detected millions of exploitation attempts within hours of disclosure. The PHP Foundation has already warned of a third RCE (CVE-2026-115560) with no patch yet.
sections.whyItMatters: The two stories are the same story: AI compresses the gap between a public vulnerability and a fully compromised identity provider from weeks to hours, and the vulnerable surface is the boring runtime underneath a third of the web. Defenders built alerting for human-paced intrusions. Against paced, rotating, AI-driven scanning, threshold-based detection mostly stops working — which is exactly what Kumagai was describing.

sections.heading: Moonshot opens Kimi K3 at 2.8 trillion parameters, and trims its hacking skill
sections.body:
Moonshot AI unveiled Kimi K3 on Friday, a 2.8 trillion-parameter model it describes as the largest open-weight system and the first open model to approach the 3 trillion mark, per The Asahi Shimbun. It carries a 1 million-token context window and is aimed at long-horizon coding and knowledge work.

The benchmarks matter more than the parameter count. Asahi reports Arena.ai ranked Kimi K3 first in a web-interface-building test, Vals AI placed it second behind Anthropic's Fable 5 and ahead of GPT-5.6 Sol, and Artificial Analysis judged it comparable to GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8 on multi-step tasks. The launch came a month after Anthropic's Fable and Mythos models were withdrawn by the US government over security concerns, per Asahi's reporting.

There is a discrepancy between the published model and the announced release. Moonshot said Saturday it had reduced the cyber-offensive capabilities of Kimi K3.1 Pro — described as a '3-trillion-parameter-class' open-weight model with a 1-million-token context — before publishing weights due November 4, stripping cyber data from training and applying reinforcement changes, per AFP. Asahi's Kimi K3 and the upcoming K3.1 Pro are related but not identical releases.

Meanwhile China's export machinery is catching up to its open-weight strategy. Reuters reported MiniMax completed technology export registration with China's Commerce Ministry for open-source release and overseas licensing of certain recently released and upcoming models — the formal channel through which Beijing now polices which Chinese frontier weights leave the country.
sections.whyItMatters: A 2.8-trillion-parameter open-weight model that ranks second behind a US frontier system resets the assumption that open weights trail closed ones by six months. It also makes the export-registration regime a real control point: Beijing is now the gatekeeper for open weights that anyone can download — a position no other government holds.

sections.heading: SpaceX stops taking new Falcon 9 reservations as Xona builds a GPS alternative
sections.body:
Prospective satellite operators can reportedly no longer place new commercial reservations for SpaceX's Falcon 9, with officials from about six companies saying separately they were unable to make new bookings, according to MSN/Bing News reporting. The effect is a narrower launch market at the moment demand for LEO capacity is climbing.

The same week showed what is filling the gap. Xona launched six satellites on SpaceX's Bandwagon rideshare mission — the largest customer on the flight — with four built by Aerospacelab supporting initial beta service in multiple countries from early 2027, per Via Satellite. Xona then announced a $250 million Series D on October 22 led by Future Ventures, valuing the company at $2.45 billion. It holds FCC approval, granted in August, for a constellation of more than 250 satellites.

Pulsar, Xona's system, broadcasts L-band signals — the same band as GPS — from low Earth orbit, which lets it be integrated into existing GPS receivers. The company claims centimetre-level precision and signals up to 100 times more powerful than GPS, targeting aviation, logistics, critical infrastructure and defense. CEO Brian Manning framed the funding as matching in-orbit capacity with manufacturing scale.
sections.whyItMatters: Launch access is being rationed by the same company that now operates the dominant LEO communications constellation, which puts satellite operators in a position where one vendor's capacity decisions shape what gets into orbit. Xona is the more interesting counter-signal: a commercial, receiver-compatible navigation layer that could give aviation and defence a second source of position and timing independent of state GNSS systems.

sections.heading: Taiwan builds a rare-earth line while its champion redesigns around the shortage
sections.body:
Taiwan's Industrial Technology Research Institute plans a rare-earth demonstration plant producing 500 tonnes annually, targeting about half of national demand by end-2030, per the Taipei Times. Construction is targeted for end-2028 with process refinement to follow — a roughly 100-fold increase over ITRI's current experimental line of about 5 tonnes a year.

Downstream, TSMC is asking equipment suppliers to develop factory-automation motors that do not use rare-earth materials, according to Reuters reporting from October 22. The effort is early-stage — a design question put to toolmakers rather than a procurement order — but it is the first sign of a major chipmaker engineering around Chinese export controls at the component level rather than inventorying against them.

The trigger remains live. China defended its rare-earth export curbs on Japan by citing 'remilitarization' concerns, per Anadolu Agency, responding to a Financial Times report that Tokyo had sought US help over a looming yttrium shortage threatening automotive, aerospace and chip industries.
sections.whyItMatters: Substitution at the motor level takes years and will not cover demand in the interim, but it is the route that actually ends dependency — unlike stockpiling. Taiwan's 500-tonne target also reframes rare earths from an upstream mining problem to a midstream processing one, where the technical barrier, not the ore, is what China controls.

bottomLine: Today's most expensive deal is also the least conventional: Japan is paying up to $21 billion for two New York fabs it will not own, the US government is converting grants into a 7% stake in the operator, and Abu Dhabi's Mubadala keeps control. It works only because all three want the output. In Japan, the state's new offensive cyber law met its first real test and hesitated — a private company asked for countermeasures and was told there is no mechanism for requests. That hesitation looks worse in light of Unit 42's finding that an AI agent took a European government entity from initial exploit to MFA secrets in two hours. And on model policy, Moonshot's 2.8-trillion-parameter open release, with export registration now a formal Beijing gate, shows open weights are no longer a lagging branch of the frontier.
sources: Reuters (via Miami Herald), 247WallSt, NYT, BigGo, OfficeChai, Keio University / Sasakawa Peace Foundation commentary, The Hacker News / Palo Alto Networks Unit 42, CYFIRMA, Bitsight, Cloudflare, The Asahi Shimbun, AFP, Via Satellite, MSN/Bing News, Taipei Times, Anadolu Agency, Financial Times (via Anadolu)
